title: Türkiye gained export share alongside China, with sharply different outcomes in apparel and steel
bank: Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye
summary: Growth in import markets explains most of Türkiye’s export gains in the markets it shared with China between 2021 and 2025. Turkish exports rose by USD 36.9 billion. Holding Türkiye’s initial market share constant, growth in destination markets would have contributed USD 28.6 billion. A net improvement in share supplied the remaining USD 8.3 billion. China’s own expansion therefore did not entail an aggregate Turkish loss across the sample. For investors assessing individual exporters, the result turns on which goods and destinations generated the gains (Box 2.4, Table 1).

The authors use importing countries’ UN Comtrade data and define a market as a four-digit Harmonized System product in a particular destination. The demand component is the change in the market’s import value multiplied by Türkiye’s 2021 share. The share component is the change in Türkiye’s share multiplied by the market’s 2025 import value. The components sum exactly to the change in export value. The exercise covers the shared markets defined in the table footnote and excludes precious metals and stones under HS chapter 71. Because the accounting uses dollar values, both quantities and unit values can move the result. Its demand component measures import expenditure at a fixed initial share, rather than a separately identified real demand shock.

Netting conceals large changes in opposite directions. In markets where Türkiye gained share, the share component contributed USD 55.3 billion. Where it lost share, the contribution was minus USD 47 billion. Some exports could still rise where Türkiye became less competitive by this measure, because the destination market grew fast enough. Grouping the same observations by China’s performance produces another informative split. Where China gained share, Turkish gains of USD 35.3 billion outweighed losses of USD 31.2 billion. Where China lost share, Türkiye gained a net USD 4.2 billion. Both countries can gain when third suppliers lose ground (Chart 1).

Among the ten largest Turkish product groups, land vehicles gained about USD 6.3 billion through share changes. Electrical equipment and machinery also gained. Knitted and non-knitted apparel together lost USD 6.1 billion and iron and steel lost USD 2.7 billion. The authors then narrow the comparison to specific product–destination markets where Türkiye lost share, before offsetting against its wins elsewhere. Within those apparel markets Vietnam gained USD 6.3 billion, Cambodia USD 4.8 billion and Bangladesh USD 3.8 billion, while China itself lost USD 3.5 billion. In the corresponding steel markets China gained USD 9.0 billion. These last numbers refer to the competitors’ gains and losses in a selected set of markets. They cannot be subtracted from Türkiye’s all-market sector totals (Charts 2–4).

The implication for an export outlook is that a broad forecast of Chinese market penetration could obscure two different risks. Turkish steel lost ground where China was particularly successful, whereas South and Southeast Asian producers were more prominent in the apparel losses. The decomposition does not identify who won any particular contract, whether a Turkish supplier cut margins to defend share, or how much future export income would accrue to local producers.

questions.question: Did the sectors gaining dollar share also gain physical volume and margin?
questions.detail: The decomposition mixes quantities and prices. Customs quantities and unit values by destination, matched to company segment margins, would distinguish improved market access from product mix or price inflation. The difference matters for cash-flow forecasts.

questions.question: How exposed are the apparent winners to a slowdown in their largest destinations?
questions.detail: Destination import growth generated most of the aggregate dollar gain. Reweight the product–destination cells using projected import demand and test concentration in vehicles and electrical equipment before translating historical share gains into revenue growth.

questions.question: Which competitors actually replaced Turkish suppliers?
questions.detail: The sector charts condition on Turkish losses but do not match contracts. More granular customs data, order books and procurement awards could identify substitution, quality differences and customer switches. That evidence would determine whether Chinese steel and Asian apparel require different competitive responses.
